x_to_y: This edge encodes that changes in \(x\) cause changes in \(y\), i.e., intervening on \(x\) would shift the distribution/level of \(y\) through the mechanism implied by the application (prices affecting demand, schooling affecting wages, etc.). The main threats to a valid causal estimate are omitted confounders that affect both \(x\) and \(y\), reverse causality (if \(y\) also feeds back into \(x\)), and selection/measurement issues that make observed \(x\) differ from the true treatment. Next, a researcher should articulate the specific channel linking \(x\) to \(y\), draw the full DAG to identify a credible adjustment set (or an instrument/natural experiment), and run balance/placebo or pre-trend checks to assess whether variation in \(x\) is plausibly exogenous.
y_to_z: This edge encodes that changes in \(y\) cause changes in \(z\), i.e., \(y\) is an upstream determinant of the outcome \(z\) in the economic system (for example, a policy or input \(y\) shifting behavior or performance \(z\)). The main risks to a credible estimate are confounding (an omitted variable jointly affecting \(y\) and \(z\)), reverse causality if \(z\) also influences \(y\), and post-treatment bias if you condition on mediators or colliders downstream of \(y\). Next, the researcher should map and justify the adjustment set implied by the DAG, verify that plausible backdoor paths are blocked without conditioning on post-\(y\) variables, and run sensitivity/placebo checks (e.g., pre-trends or negative controls) consistent with the proposed causal direction.
